body: The marine layer burned off at eleven, and Hollis 302 has its window back: hard blue sea all the way up the glass, one container ship pinned to the horizon, a pelican going by at desk height like it’s late for something. The radiator knocks anyway; Yusuf says it’s load-bearing.

Jack is early, in the navy blazer, with the Williams and the Nagel stapled together out of the course packet and Flannery O’Connor riding in his back pocket, spine still white. There is gold in his left eyebrow. Theo’s face soap got most of the fleur-de-lis off last night; the rest went down into the scar, a fleck of Sully’s that catches when he turns his head.

Yusuf comes in with his water bottle empty on principle, twenty-four days into the fast, and drops into the chair beside him. Before anything else he says, “He called. Yesterday.” Tariq, from Helmand: four minutes on a line that sounded like it was coming through a box fan. “He complained about the food the whole time. Which means he’s fine. When he says the food’s good, I worry.” “Good,” Jack says, and Yusuf nods at the table like they’ve agreed on a measurement.

At 1:01 Lena comes in from the 12:10 with the mantilla still in her hand, folding it down into the OCTAVIA tote on top of the Greek grammar as she sits across the oak from him. Keds. One strand of gold Sully’s beads still on under the cardigan, against the chain. She doesn’t say hello. She says, settling, “God’s cure for snakebite was to make them look at the snake.” “Good afternoon, Broussard.” “Numbers twenty-one. The bronze serpent on the pole. Father Osei in red — very dramatic, you’d have hated how much you liked it. Where were you?” “Reading Nagel.” She takes her own copy out, flattened and flagged in three colors. “Then you looked at the snake too.”

At 1:07 Hale comes in and sets down the roster and nothing else. The linen jacket, and the wine is back on the cuff; whatever happened to last Wednesday’s clean sleeve, it didn’t last the weekend. He doesn’t sit. He stands at the sea window with his hands in his pockets, and there’s a color in his face that isn’t only the broken veins — a man walking into his own house.

“Week three,” he says. “Williams, ‘Moral Luck.’ Nagel, ‘Moral Luck.’ Two very clever men and one very good title between them.” Caleb, who has the Post-its out already and is glowing like a kid in the front pew, can’t hold it. “He wrote his doctorate on this.” “Under the long shadow of a better man,” Hale says, not turning around. “Mr. Hargrove has read my jacket copy.” Caleb glows anyway.

Then Hale does turn, and finds Jack. “Last week Mr. Costigan informed us that you don’t get out of a thing by forgetting it. This week we find out whether you can get *into* one by accident.” He lets the room wait for it. “Two men drive home from the same party. Only one of them hits anybody.”

He gives them the rest of it slowly. The same party. The same number of drinks — four, let’s say; large men, long party. The same road home, the same bend in it, the same dark, the same bad half-second where the wheel goes soft in the hands. In front of the first car there is nothing but road. In front of the second car a child runs out after a ball. “Same men,” Hale says. “Same choices. Same everything, up to a small boy and a red ball, which neither of them ordered. Is the second man worse?”
Jack has the Nagel open to the paragraph and doesn’t need it.

Caleb goes first, because he always goes first. “It’s luck all the way down. Neither of them’s anything. They’re weather. *Selah*.” Yusuf lifts his head off his arms. “In Islam there’s a word for this,” he says. “*Diya*. You kill somebody by mistake, you owe the family. Blood money. And if you can’t pay it, you fast two months straight.” He considers the empty bottle. “So the second driver owes something the first one doesn’t. I’m on month one by accident.” The table laughs. Yusuf glances down the oak at Jack — the same look he gave him across the lounge on Wednesday night, over *in that room* — and puts his head back down on his arms.
Lena doesn’t raise her hand; she never has. “The same,” she says. “Same sin. Same will, same act, same four drinks. The child is the second man’s grief. It isn’t his sin.”
“Mr. Costigan,” Hale says, “you’re making a face.”

“He’s worse.” He hears the weight on it only once it’s across the table — harder than anything he decided to say, hard enough that the chemistry kid looks up from the highlighter. Lena’s eyes come to him and hold.
Hale looks from one of them to the other, and the pleasure on him is undisguised. “Designated antagonists,” he says. “Ten minutes a round. Win me something.”
She pushes her sleeves up. Both of them, to the elbow, one and then the other.

“Kant,” Lena says, “and I want it in the minutes that I hate agreeing with a Prussian. The good will shines like a jewel by its own light — even if it never gets anything done, even if a stepmotherly nature leaves it nothing to work with, it has its whole worth in itself.” She turns a page she doesn’t need to look at. “And if y’all prefer a Dominican: an act gets its moral species from its object, its end and its circumstances. *Prima secundae*, question eighteen. Not from what a four-year-old does next. The second man’s will is exactly as rotten as the first man’s will. Nothing that runs into the road changes what he chose at the bar.” She looks down the oak, past Jack, to Hale. “If a gust of wind can make you a murderer, Professor, then ‘murderer’ is a weather report.”
Caleb says “*Dude*” under his breath, reverently. Hale makes a small mark on the roster.

choices.text: Every legal system that ever existed gives the second driver years and the first one a fine. All of them wrong?
response: “Hammurabi. Rome. Ohio,” Jack says. “Nobody’s ever been charged with vehicular almost. All of them wrong?”

“All of them *afraid*,” she says, and then — he watches her decide to pay for it — she grants it. The law has to count bodies. It can’t see wills; it only sees what’s lying in the road. “So it punishes what it can find. That’s a confession about the law, Costigan. It isn’t one about the man.” Behind her Hale uncaps a marker, writes LAW on the whiteboard in letters a foot high, and underlines it twice, which in this room is a point.

choices.text: “In Youngstown ‘murderer’ is a weather report. Lake-effect.”
response: The table goes up. The San Diego boys laugh in harmony; Yusuf laughs into his sleeve. Lena laughs too, out loud and without apology, and keeps her jewel exactly where it was. “Cute,” she says. “Hold that thought, put a coat on it. Then move, Costigan.”

choices.text: “I’ll give you the act. Same act.”
response: She wasn’t ready for it. She had the next thing loaded — he can see it go back in the chamber — and she sets it down instead and banks what he’s given her, without a flourish. “Noted,” she says, “and appreciated.” Then, because she can’t entirely help herself: “The act was always mine. But I’ll sign for it.”

choices.text: Williams’s lorry driver. Ask him if he feels like a bystander. He doesn’t, and he shouldn’t — he had his hands on the wheel, and that’s a fact about him.
response: “Williams,” Jack says. “The driver who runs over a kid through no fault of his own feels different from anybody standing on the curb. Even the guy in the passenger seat. And Williams says something would be wrong with him if he didn’t.”
Hale turns from the window, pleased against his will and not bothering to hide it. “*Agent-regret*. He’s read the footnotes.” Lena: “Regret isn’t guilt.” Jack: “Tell the lorry driver.”

body: Round two she brings the big gun, and she brings it from memory. “Thomas,” she says. “*Prima secundae*, question twenty, article five. Whether the consequences of an act add to its goodness or its malice.” Her pen taps the oak once per clause. “If they’re foreseen, yes. If they aren’t foreseen — then only if they follow from the act of itself, and in most cases. What follows by accident, and seldom, adds nothing. Not a feather.” She folds her hands. “The child is *per accidens*, Professor.”
At the window Hale turns his head and raises his eyebrows at Jack: *well?*

choices.text: Read the rest. *Per se and in most cases.* A drunk car hitting somebody isn’t an accident. It’s what drunk cars do.
response: “*Ut in pluribus*,” Jack says. “Four drinks and a dark bend. You don’t get to call that *seldom*, Broussard. Ask anybody who drives Market Street on a Friday.”

Her eyebrows go up — the best Thomist move he’s made all season, and from the Augustinian side of the table — and for a second she looks like she might actually applaud. Then she turns it around in her hands and hands it back to him loaded. “Then the first driver’s a murderer who got lucky.” Caleb: “*Ooh*.”

choices.text: “Aquinas never drove Market Street at closing time.”
response: A laugh around the table, and she rides it. “Aquinas walked from Naples to Paris, Costigan. On foot. In a habit. More than once.” She lets the room picture it. “He knew what roads do to people.” The table gives her that one, and Hale, at the window, gives it to her too, with one lifted finger.

choices.text: “Miss Broussard walks out of things. Songs. Diners. Maybe if you’re not in the room, it didn’t happen.”
choices.key: In Hale’s seminar you told Lena she walks out of things.
response: It wins the point. He knows it as it leaves him: it’s the kind of sentence that wins rooms. Hale laughs — one bark, delighted with nobody but himself — and says, “Oh, there it is. Somebody’s been keeping notes,” and half the table looks at Lena, because all of them were here the first Monday, when Hale told them about the Anchor.

Lena squares the pages of the Williams against the oak, so the edges agree. Then she squares them again. They already agree. She keeps squaring them. “That’s a fair hit, Mr. Costigan,” she says, very pleasantly, without looking up from the stack.

choices.text: “He didn’t choose the kid.”
response: “No,” she says. “Neither did the kid.”
She leaves his concession where he put it, and takes nothing extra off the table on the way past. Hale writes something on the roster and crosses it out.

body: Then she stops.

Not the round — she’s still in the round. But the machete goes down on the table, and her sleeves come down to her wrists, and her hand goes up to the medal and holds it, the thin gold oval worn soft between her finger and thumb. She’s looking at him. Not at Hale, not at the table. Of everyone in Hollis 302, she is the only one who knows the name of a prison outside Warren, Ohio.

body.text: “Then what does he owe, Mr. Costigan?” The formal name stays on, and everything else about the question is gentler than anything she’s said all hour. “If he’s worse. What does he owe, and to whom, and for how long?”
body.else: “Then what does he owe, Costigan?” Quieter. The theater gone out of it. “If he’s worse. What does he owe, and to whom, and for how long?”

body: The radiator knocks. Caleb’s pen stops over his Post-it.

choices.text: “Everything. He stands up and says ‘I did that.’ He doesn’t get to go home. Nobody gets to take it for him.”
choices.key: You said the unlucky driver owes everything — that nobody gets to take it for him.
response: He says it to her and it goes to the whole room. He means every word, and he puts every word of it down on the oak like a man laying bricks: he stands up, he says *I did that*, he doesn’t get to go home, nobody — nobody — gets to take it for him.

Nobody laughs. Caleb has stopped writing altogether. Lena’s hand is still at her collar; the point goes past her untouched, and after a moment she looks down at her own pages. Hale has turned all the way around from the window. He looks at Jack without any wit in his face at all, the way he looked at the sea window the first afternoon. Jack finds his palms flat on the oak, pressing, and makes himself lift them.

choices.text: “He owes the kid’s mother the truth. That’s all he’s got. The rest isn’t his to pay.”
choices.key: You said the driver owes the child’s mother the truth — and the rest isn’t his to pay.
response: He gives it to her plainly, no flourish. Lena lets go of the medal. She studies him across the oak as if he’s a line of Greek that’s just come clear.
“That’s the first thing you’ve said all hour I believe,” she says.
Hale says, “Hm,” and makes no mark at all.

choices.text: “Five to ten. Less with good behavior.”
choices.key: You answered Lena’s question with a sentencing joke.
response: The room laughs — the San Diego boys, the Palo Alto girl, Caleb slapping the oak — and it’s a good laugh; it’s timed. Lena doesn’t laugh. She lets go of the medal and says, to the table and not to him, “The child doesn’t get good behavior.”
The laugh runs on around her for a while and runs out, and when it has run out she is still looking at him, and he would give a good deal to have the sentence back in his mouth.

choices.text: The Misfit: *“I can’t make what all I done wrong fit what all I gone through in punishment.”* It never fits. He pays anyway.
choices.key: You answered Lena with the Misfit: it never fits, and he pays anyway.
response: He has it by heart; it’s been riding in his back pocket since Sunday morning. “*I call myself The Misfit because I can’t make what all I done wrong fit what all I gone through in punishment.*” He sets the paperback on the oak. “It never fits. Not for anybody. Too much or too little. He pays anyway, because the paying isn’t math. It’s the only thing he can still do with his hands.”

Hale puts a hand over his eyes. “Flannery O’Connor,” he says, “in my seminar. Someone open a window.” One of the San Diego boys actually gets up and does it, and the room fills with the sound of the surf and the smell of kelp and somebody’s mower down on the Commons.
Lena lets go of the medal. “The Misfit shoots a grandmother,” she says quietly. “Pick a better saint.”

body: Her last move, and the sleeves go back up. She puts both hands flat on her pages and leans into it, and her voice gets that long Gulf roll it gets when she’s building to the end of something.

“Y’all keep saying *luck* like it’s a thing in the world. Like it’s a fifth guest at the party. It isn’t.” She looks at Caleb, kindly, and then at Hale, not. “There’s no luck, Professor. There’s providence, and there’s mercy, and both drivers need the second one.”

It should be the end of the round. It isn’t, because Hale isn’t refereeing anymore. He comes off the window and stands at the head of the table with his fingertips on the oak, and when he speaks it is very soft and very clear, every consonant cut.
“Forgiven by whom, Miss Broussard? The child is dead. The only one with standing to forgive is the one who can’t.”
The radiator knocks. Lena’s face doesn’t move. Only the color does, high on her cheekbones, and Jack has seen that once before, at the end of the harbor pier, when she said *four days*.
“That’s why it has to be God, Professor,” she says. “He’s the only one who can speak for the dead.”

Hale doesn’t answer. He looks past her, out the sea window, at the ship that hasn’t moved and the water that hasn’t stopped, and the room waits for him, and he goes on looking. Then, without turning his head: “Mr. Costigan. Last word.”

choices.text: “Then why’d He let the kid run out?” — Epicurus, Hale’s own Tuesday, turned on her.
response: “If He’s providence,” Jack says, “He was on that road. Able and not willing, or willing and not able. Pick one.” It’s Hale’s own Tuesday, handed back to him with the bow still on it, and Hale’s mouth moves at one corner.

“Ask Job,” Lena says, and it’s a good answer, and she gives him the whirlwind like she’s reading it off the inside of her eyelids: “*Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Have you commanded the morning since your days began?*” She sits back. Out the window the ship still hasn’t moved.

choices.text: “Both need it. Yeah.”
response: She nods once — the nod she gives the end of the Creed, *and the life of the world to come*, settled. Caleb looks back and forth between them as if he’s walked in on a family. Yusuf murmurs, “Factor of safety,” and nobody asks him what he means.

choices.text: “Then the lucky one owes God a thank-you note.”
response: “He owes Him a *life*,” Lena says, without missing a step. “The note’s extra.” Yusuf, from inside his folded arms: “Inshallah, in triplicate.” The table breaks up, and even Hale’s shoulders move once.

choices.text: Hale told four hundred people the bill always gets paid and never by the theologian. She just said God pays it. Which is it — is He the theologian, or the one who pays?
response: “Last Tuesday,” Jack says, “in Sandoval, the Professor told four hundred people the problem of evil is a bill, and it’s never the theologian who pays it. So which is your God, Broussard? The theologian or the one who pays?”
Hale turns from the window to watch her answer. She doesn’t need long. “He’s the one who pays,” she says. “You wrote it. Page one.” She doesn’t have to look it up. She’s the one who bled on it.

body.text: Hale gives it to Jack, and makes a production of it. “Mr. Costigan has dragged the Old Testament into the twenty-first century by its beard.” Caleb claps, three times, alone. Three–one on the season, if anybody’s counting, and Jack is. Across the oak Lena packs her pages into the tote without hurrying, and as she stands she says, low, just for him, “You argued that like it was yours.”
He gave her the mother first. The rest of the hour he took off her by force, but that one he handed over, and she slides her chair in like somebody who noticed.

There’s no winner. Hale tries to give it to Lena on the last move, and Lena won’t take it. “No,” she says. “He gave me the mother. That was the right one to give me.” She gives the round back across the oak like change. Hale throws up his hands. “Two Catholics agreeing about mercy. I’ve lost the room.” Two–one on the season, and a draw, and it feels like more than either.

The room had a lovely time. Caleb is still laughing at something from round two. Hale declines to score it at all. “That wasn’t a disputation,” he says. “That was a revue. I’ll send you both a bill for the hall.” No decision; two–one on the season, still. Lena caps her pen and gives Jack a look that says *next Monday*.

Hale doesn’t make them wait. “Miss Broussard,” he says, “by a weather report.” Lena accepts it with a small nod, no fuss. Two–two on the season. She packs up humming “When the Saints Go Marching In,” under her breath, in the wrong key on purpose.

Hale gives it to Lena, and Lena takes it, and thanks him, and is courteous to Mr. Costigan in a voice you could chill a bottle in. Two–two on the season, and it doesn’t feel like two of anything. Hale surveys the table with real satisfaction. “Blood on the floor,” he says. “Somebody fetch the spaniel a mop.”

body: “Wednesday,” Hale says to all of them. “Two pages. Prove the thing you least believe you can prove.” He’s back at the window already, his back to the room.

body.text: Chairs scrape. The San Diego boys go out arguing about tonight’s Chargers game. Lena is gone before Jack has the Nagel in his bag.
body.else: Chairs scrape. The San Diego boys go out arguing about tonight’s Chargers game. Lena goes out ahead, tote on her shoulder, while Jack is still getting the Nagel into his bag.

body: The O’Connor has slid under his chair. By the time he’s fished it out, the room is empty except for him and the radiator and the man at the window. Hale hasn’t turned around. His hands are in his pockets, and the wine on the cuff is the color of an old scab in the afternoon light.
“Do you think the lucky one sleeps, Mr. Costigan?”

choices.text: “No.”
response: “No,” Jack says.
Hale stands there with it. Down on the water the ship has finally started to move, so slowly you can only tell by the gap behind it. “No,” Hale says, to the glass.

choices.text: “I think he counts trains.”
response: It’s meant as a joke, and it leaves his mouth as something else.

Hale turns around. He looks at Jack over the top of the empty table — the blazer, the white-spined paperback, the gold in the eyebrow — and for a moment he looks his age, and then older than that. “Do you,” he says. It isn’t a question.

choices.text: “Do you?”
response: Hale laughs, short and real. “Like a baby, Mr. Costigan,” he says. “Up every two hours, crying.”
He doesn’t turn around. He lifts one hand off his pocket and moves it, a small Oxford flick toward the door, a waiter dismissed with affection. Jack goes.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Three–one. Moral luck: mine. She said I argued it like it was mine.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–one, and a draw. I gave her the right point. She gave the round back.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–one. Moral luck: no decision. Hale called it a revue.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–two. Moral luck: hers, by a weather report.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–two. Moral luck: hers. I won a point I shouldn’t have.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Knew my face from the Anchor before he knew my name. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps.

s06.slug: MONDAY · 2:31 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE CLOISTER WALK
body: The Hollis cloister is all red tile and shadow and bougainvillea, the magenta kind with the paper petals, drifting onto the walk and lying there like confetti after somebody else’s wedding. Up on Ferrer Tower the carillon is finishing the half hour, off-key, the Westminster chimes with one bell flat for as long as anyone at Marisol can remember. The stone gives back the heat of the day.

body.text: Lena has waited. She’s at the far end of the walk, under the last arch, the tote on one shoulder and one Ked up on the base of a pillar, and she watches him come the whole length of it.
body.else: Lena hasn’t waited. She’s ahead of him, walking fast in the Keds, and he has to lengthen his stride to catch her halfway down the walk. She lets him catch her, and keeps her pace.

body.text: “You argued that like it was yours, Mr. Costigan,” she says, as if she were reading it off a form.
“I meant it,” she says, first. “In there. You argued that like it was yours.”
“You argued that like it was yours,” she says, first.

body: A gardener’s blower starts up somewhere past the arch and stops again. She waits for his answer the way she waits for the Gospel, standing.

choices.text: “It’s about my brother.”
choices.key: You told Lena the argument was about your brother.

response.text: “I figured,” she says. “I was watching you.” She adjusts the strap of the tote. “Mr. Costigan.”
response.else: “I figured,” she says. “I was watching you.” Then she falls in beside him, close enough that the tote bumps his elbow every third step, and they walk out from under the last arch into the sun.

response.text: When he starts on what he said in there — “Broussard, about the — ” — she has the answer ready before he’s found the noun. “I’m perfectly fine, Mr. Costigan.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and closes on it. They walk the rest of the cloister like two people who happen to have the same class next.

choices.text: “It’s about me.”
choices.key: You told Lena the argument was about you.
response: She looks at him for a while, under the arch, with the bougainvillea coming down between them. Then she nods, slowly, as if he’s confirmed something she’d already written in the margin. “Because you got out,” she says, “and he didn’t.”

response.text: Even cold, she gives him the rest of it. “The one who got out doesn’t owe the one who didn’t his whole life, Mr. Costigan. He owes him letters.”
response.else: “The one who got out doesn’t owe the one who didn’t his whole life, Jack,” she says. “He owes him letters.”

response: Jack looks at a petal on the tile. “Letters,” he says. “Okay.”

response.text: When he starts on what he said in there — “Broussard, about the — ” — she has the answer ready before he’s found the noun. “I’m perfectly fine, Mr. Costigan.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and closes on it. They walk the rest of the cloister like two people who happen to have the same class next.

choices.text: “I like winning.”
choices.key: You told Lena you just like winning.
response: “Sure,” she says. “Who doesn’t.” She lets him have it — openly, deliberately, so he can watch her do it. It’s a receipt, folded once, and they both know what’s printed on it.

response.text: When he starts on what he said in there — “Broussard, about the — ” — she has the answer ready before he’s found the noun. “I’m perfectly fine, Mr. Costigan.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and closes on it. They walk the rest of the cloister like two people who happen to have the same class next.

choices.text: “What I said in there. I’m sorry.”
choices.key: You apologized to Lena for what you said in the seminar.
response: She makes him wait. She makes him wait the whole length of the cloister, back the way they came, past every arch and every drift of petals and the drinking fountain that hasn’t worked since the Nixon administration, him a half step behind her the entire way. At the far end she stops and turns.
“Apology noted, Costigan.”
Plain Costigan, no mister. She hitches the tote higher on her shoulder and starts back toward the sun, and this time she slows down enough for him.

s06b.slug: MONDAY · 2:39 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE CLOISTER WALK
body: His hip buzzes. He gets the RAZR open and tips the cracked screen until it finds the one angle where it still lights. It’s 5:39 in Youngstown. School let out two hours ago.

body.text: a girl in religion said im the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. bc of danny. everybody laughed. mrs d said ladies and kept going

body: He reads it. He reads *bc of danny* again by itself. Somewhere on the Commons a frisbee lands and somebody cheers, and the bougainvillea keeps coming down, and his thumb is on the hinge, pressing the crack.

body.text: He must look like something, because Lena stops. The chill is still in her voice. It isn’t anywhere else. “What happened, Mr. Costigan?”
body.else: He must look like something, because Lena stops. “Jack. What happened?”

choices.text: Hand her the phone.
choices.key: You showed Lena your sister’s text.
response: He holds it out. She takes it in both hands and tilts it until the screen lights for her, and reads it, and reads it again. “Gina,” she says, from the top of the screen. “Your sister.” “Fifteen. Ursuline.” She closes the phone gently and gives it back to him, and the girl who did Lincoln–Douglas at thirteen comes up into her face like a fighter coming off the stool.

“When they go personal, you don’t defend. You name it. Tell her to say his name — just his name, *Danny* — and then look at that girl until she looks away. Don’t explain. Don’t argue. Make her hear it’s a person.”

response.text: When she gets to *personal*, she’s looking at the phone in his hand, not at him.

choices.text: “My sister. Some girl called her the convict’s sister.”
choices.key: You told Lena what they’re calling your sister.
response: “What’s her name?” “Gina.” “And the girl’s?” “Don’t know.” “Find out,” Lena says. “So you can pray for her.” She lets that land before the rest. “And then so Gina can destroy her.”

Then the girl who did Lincoln–Douglas at thirteen comes up into her face like a fighter coming off the stool. “When they go personal, you don’t defend. You name it. Tell her to say his name — just his name, *Danny* — and then look at that girl until she looks away. Don’t explain. Don’t argue. Make her hear it’s a person.”

response.text: When she gets to *personal*, she’s looking past him.

choices.text: Close the phone. “Family stuff.”
response: He folds the RAZR shut, and the click is louder than it should be in the cloister. “Family stuff.”

response.text: Lena looks at the closed phone and then at him. “I took ‘mostly’ back off you on a pier, Mr. Costigan,” she says. “Don’t make me start a collection.”
response.else: Lena looks at the closed phone and then at him. “I took ‘mostly’ back off you on a pier, Costigan,” she says. “Don’t make me start a collection.”

response: He breathes in. “…Later.”
She weighs it. “Okay,” she says. “Later.” She walks with him out to the Commons and asks nothing more. He closed that door himself; they can both hear it.
